hook: A school district starts a mentoring program, and this year's random sample shows 14% of students chronically absent, down from 18% last year. The superintendent wants to announce that absence has dropped. A complete significance test says whether the data back her up, and it also says what she still cannot claim.

prereq.q: For $H_0: p = 0.18$, $H_a: p < 0.18$, $n = 450$ and $\hat{p} = 0.14$, which is the test statistic?
prereq.why: Statistic minus null value, over the standard deviation computed with $p_0 = 0.18$.

prereq.q: Which hypotheses fit "has the proportion gone down from 18%?"
prereq.why: The equals sign goes in $H_0$; "gone down" gives a one-sided alternative about $p$.

figure.caption: State, plan, do, conclude: a complete one-sample z test for a proportion, with every part written out.

chain.effect: the result is too unusual under $H_0$: reject $H_0$, and there is convincing evidence for $H_a$
fail to reject $H_0$: there is not convincing evidence for $H_a$ (which does not make $H_0$ true)

chain.cause: The data come from a random sample
chain.effect: the conclusion applies to the population that was sampled

chain.cause: There was no random assignment to treatments
chain.effect: the test can show a change but not what caused it

ideas: Four steps: State ($H_0$, $H_a$, $\alpha$, $p$ defined), Plan (procedure, conditions), Do ($z$, p-value), Conclude.
Conclusion: "Because the p-value of __ is less than $\alpha$ = __, we reject $H_0$. There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of all __ is __ than __."
Fail to reject: "there is not convincing evidence that ...", still naming the direction of $H_a$. Never "accept $H_0$" or "prove".
A two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$ almost always rejects when $p_0$ is outside the 95% interval, and fails to reject when it is inside.
Random sampling lets you generalize; only random assignment lets you claim cause.

misconception.wrong: The p-value of 0.38 is greater than 0.05, so we accept $H_0$: the proportion has not changed.
misconception.right: Fail to reject $H_0$: there is not convincing evidence that the proportion has changed. The data are consistent with $H_0$, but a test cannot show that $H_0$ is true.

summary: A complete test runs state, plan, do, conclude. It states hypotheses about $p$ with $\alpha$, names the one-sample z test for a proportion and checks random, 10% and large counts with $p_0$, computes $z$ and the p-value, then concludes: compare the p-value with $\alpha$, reject or fail to reject $H_0$, and say whether there is convincing evidence for $H_a$ about the true proportion of all ..., in context. Never accept $H_0$, and claim cause only from a randomized experiment.
